title: Widefield vs confocal
objective: Explain how a confocal pinhole produces optical sections.

steps.title: The out-of-focus haze
steps.body: A **[[widefield microscopy|widefield]]** scope lights the whole sample, so light from above and below your focal plane blurs the image. A **[[confocal microscopy|confocal]]** adds a **pinhole** that blocks out-of-focus light, so only the in-focus plane reaches the detector — an *optical section*.

steps.prompt: What does the confocal pinhole do?
options: Blocks out-of-focus light to give a clean optical section
Makes the excitation laser substantially more powerful
Narrows the beam so only the focal plane gets excited
Filters the excitation light out of the emitted light
steps.explanation: The pinhole rejects light from other planes, giving thin optical sections you can stack into 3D.

variants.setup: You switch from widefield to confocal on a thick section.
variants.reveal: The pinhole removes out-of-focus blur, sharpening a thick sample.

steps.setup: You image a 50 µm section of densely labeled axons on a widefield scope and can't tell which axon is which.
steps.prompt: What do you predict confocal would do?
options: Separate the planes so the axons become distinguishable
Brighten the axons, but they would still overlap
Sharpen only the surface; deeper axons stay hazy
steps.reveal: Optical sectioning separates overlapping structures by depth, so tangled axons resolve into distinct planes.

variants.prompt: Tangled axons in a thick section image clearly on…
options: Widefield, with the lamp turned up high
Neither scope can really help with this
variants.explanation: Confocal separates depths, untangling overlapping structures.

steps.title: The cost
steps.body: Confocal scans point by point, so it's slower and the laser can bleach or photo-damage the sample. For thin, sparse samples, widefield may be faster and plenty. Match the tool to the question.
